what_its_for: Olaparib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of cancers, including ovarian cancer, breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, and prostate cancer. It works best in people whose cancer is linked to changes (mutations) in genes called BRCA1 or BRCA2. It belongs to a group of drugs called PARP inhibitors, which help stop cancer cells from repairing themselves so they die off.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablets or capsules whole with a full glass of water. You can take olaparib with or without food. Do not crush, chew, or break the tablets or capsules. Try to take your doses at the same times each day to keep the medicine working as steadily as possible.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 300 mg (two 150 mg tablets) taken twice a day, about 12 hours apart. Your doctor may lower your dose if you have side effects or certain health conditions. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regular scheduled time. Do not take a double dose to make up for the one you missed. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store olaparib at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Keep all medicines safely out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a safe drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, Seville oranges, and starfruit while taking olaparib, as they can increase the amount of medicine in your body and worsen side effects. Avoid St. John's Wort supplements because they can make olaparib less effective. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, especially certain antibiotics, antifungals, seizure medicines, or HIV medicines, as many drugs can interact with olaparib. Women who could become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Men with partners who could become pregnant should use contraception during treatment and for 3 months after. Do not breastfeed while taking olaparib.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: unusual tiredness or shortness of breath (which could be signs of low blood cell counts); easy bruising or bleeding; fever, chills, or signs of infection; coughing up blood; blood in your urine or stool; new or worsening bone pain; sudden severe headache or confusion; or any signs of a blood clot such as leg pain, swelling, or sudden chest pain. Also call your doctor if you develop a new or worsening cough or difficulty breathing, as olaparib can rarely cause serious lung problems. Tell your doctor immediately if you think you could be pregnant.
when_it_works: Olaparib begins working soon after you start taking it, but it may take several weeks to months before your doctor can measure how well it is controlling your cancer. Your doctor will use blood tests and scans to check your response to treatment. It is very important to keep taking it even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your doctor may lower your dose if you have moderate kidney problems. Olaparib is not recommended for people with severe kidney disease. Liver problems: Your doctor will monitor you closely if you have liver problems; use in severe liver disease is not recommended. Older adults (65 and older): Olaparib can be used, but you may be more sensitive to side effects, so your doctor will monitor you carefully. Pregnancy: Olaparib can harm an unborn baby and must NOT be used during pregnancy. Reliable birth control is essential. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment or for 1 month after the last dose. Children: Olaparib is not approved for use in children.
